what_its_for: Durvalumab is a type of immunotherapy medicine called a checkpoint inhibitor. It helps your immune system find and attack cancer cells. It is used to treat certain types of lung cancer (including small cell lung cancer and non-small cell lung cancer that cannot be removed by surgery), as well as certain types of liver cancer and bile duct cancer. Your doctor will explain exactly which type of cancer it is being used for in your case.
how_to_take: Durvalumab is given as an intravenous (IV) infusion, meaning it goes directly into your vein through a needle or catheter. You will receive it at a hospital, clinic, or infusion center. A nurse or healthcare provider will give you the infusion. Each infusion usually takes about 60 minutes. You will be watched closely during and after the infusion for any reactions. You do NOT take this medicine as a pill at home.
dosing: Your doctor will decide your dose based on your body weight and the type of cancer being treated. Common dosing schedules include receiving it every 2 weeks, every 3 weeks, or every 4 weeks. Your doctor may also combine it with chemotherapy or other medicines. Never try to change your dose or schedule on your own — always follow your doctor's plan.
missed_dose: Because durvalumab is given at a clinic or hospital, a healthcare team manages your schedule. If you need to miss or reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or treatment center as soon as possible. Try not to skip doses, as keeping your treatment on schedule is very important for it to work well.
storage: Durvalumab is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals at your treatment center. You do not need to store it at home. If you have any take-home supplies related to your treatment (such as other medicines), follow the storage instructions on those labels.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting durvalumab, as some may interact with it. Avoid starting any new medicines without first asking your doctor. If you have an autoimmune disease (such as lupus or Crohn's disease), make sure your doctor knows, as durvalumab can make these conditions worse. Avoid becoming pregnant while on this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose.
when_to_call_doctor: Durvalumab works by boosting your immune system, which can sometimes cause your immune system to attack healthy organs. Call your doctor RIGHT AWAY or go to an emergency room if you notice: trouble breathing or shortness of breath, chest pain or tightness, severe or persistent cough, skin rash, blistering, or peeling, yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), severe stomach pain, nausea, vomiting, or diarrhea, dark urine or very pale stools, unusual or extreme tiredness, muscle weakness, joint pain, dizziness or fainting, rapid heartbeat, severe headache, blurred or double vision, confusion or memory problems, numbness or tingling in hands or feet, increased thirst or urination, or any swelling of the face, lips, or throat during or after the infusion (infusion reaction). These can be signs of serious side effects that need immediate medical attention.
when_it_works: Durvalumab does not work overnight. It may take several weeks to months before you notice its effects. Some patients see results after a few treatment cycles, while others may take longer. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular scans and blood tests to see how well the treatment is working. Keep going to all your appointments even if you do not feel any different right away.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Durvalumab can harm an unborn baby. Do not use this medicine if you are pregnant. Use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 3 months after the last dose. Do not breastfeed during treatment and for at least 3 months after your last dose. Older adults: Durvalumab has been used safely in older adults, but your doctor will monitor you closely for side effects. Kidney or liver problems: If you have kidney or liver problems, tell your doctor before starting treatment, as this may affect how your body handles the medicine and your risk of side effects. Children: The safety and use of durvalumab in children varies by indication; your doctor will advise if it is appropriate.
